chapter_text:
CHAPTER 22 - LIFE PROCESSES - 1: NUTRITION, TRANSPORTATION, RESPIRATION AND EXCRETION

Introduction

All living organisms - from a single bacterial cell to a giant blue whale - carry out a set of basic functions that keep them alive. These essential functions are called LIFE PROCESSES. The maintenance functions that must go on continuously even when an organism is resting are nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion (along with control, coordination, growth and reproduction studied elsewhere). In this chapter we study the first four. NUTRITION supplies the body with energy-rich food and building materials. RESPIRATION breaks down that food to release usable energy. TRANSPORTATION carries materials (food, gases, wastes) to and from the cells. EXCRETION removes the harmful nitrogenous wastes produced by metabolism. Together they keep the internal environment of the body steady.

22.1 NUTRITION

Nutrition is the process of taking in food and using it for energy, growth and repair. On the basis of how organisms obtain food, nutrition is of two main types: AUTOTROPHIC (self-feeding) and HETEROTROPHIC (other-feeding).

AUTOTROPHIC NUTRITION
Autotrophs make their own food from simple inorganic raw materials. Green plants, algae and some bacteria are autotrophs. The most important autotrophic process is PHOTOSYNTHESIS - the making of food (glucose) from carbon dioxide and water using light energy trapped by the green pigment CHLOROPHYLL.
The overall equation is:

   6CO2 + 6H2O --(sunlight, chlorophyll)--> C6H12O6 + 6O2

RAW MATERIALS: carbon dioxide (taken in from the air through tiny pores called STOMATA on the leaf), water (absorbed by the roots from the soil and carried up to the leaf), sunlight (the energy source) and chlorophyll (the green pigment in the chloroplasts that traps light).
SITE: photosynthesis takes place mainly in the CHLOROPLASTS of the green cells of the leaf (the leaf is the chief food-making organ, the 'kitchen' of the plant).
STEPS: photosynthesis occurs in two stages. (1) The LIGHT REACTION (light-dependent phase): chlorophyll absorbs sunlight; the energy splits water molecules into hydrogen and oxygen (a process called photolysis). Oxygen is released as a by-product, and energy is trapped in energy-rich molecules. (2) The DARK REACTION (light-independent phase): the trapped energy is used to combine carbon dioxide with hydrogen to build glucose. Although called 'dark', this stage does not require darkness - it simply does not need light directly.
FACTORS affecting the rate of photosynthesis: light intensity, concentration of carbon dioxide, temperature and availability of water. Within limits, increasing light, CO2 and temperature increases the rate.

HETEROTROPHIC NUTRITION
Heterotrophs cannot make their own food; they depend, directly or indirectly, on autotrophs. There are three main types:
 - HOLOZOIC nutrition: taking in solid or liquid food and digesting it inside the body. Seen in most animals including humans, Amoeba and Paramecium.
 - SAPROPHYTIC (saprotrophic) nutrition: feeding on dead and decaying organic matter by secreting digestive enzymes onto it and absorbing the dissolved products. Seen in fungi (e.g. mushrooms, bread mould) and many bacteria.
 - PARASITIC nutrition: living on or inside another living organism (the host) and taking food from it, usually harming the host. Examples: Cuscuta (a parasitic plant), tapeworm, roundworm, lice and Plasmodium.

HUMAN DIGESTIVE SYSTEM
Humans show holozoic nutrition. The digestive system consists of the ALIMENTARY CANAL (a long tube from mouth to anus) and associated DIGESTIVE GLANDS.
The alimentary canal: MOUTH -> oesophagus (food pipe) -> STOMACH -> SMALL INTESTINE -> LARGE INTESTINE -> rectum -> ANUS.
Associated glands: salivary glands (in the mouth), gastric glands (in the stomach wall), the LIVER (the largest gland; secretes bile), and the PANCREAS (secretes pancreatic juice).
Steps of digestion:
 1. In the MOUTH, teeth chew the food and the salivary glands release SALIVA. Saliva contains the enzyme salivary amylase (ptyalin) which begins the digestion of starch (a carbohydrate) into maltose (a sugar).
 2. In the STOMACH, gastric glands secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid (which kills germs and provides an acidic medium), the enzyme PEPSIN (begins protein digestion) and mucus (protects the stomach lining). Churning mixes food with the juice.
 3. In the SMALL INTESTINE, digestion is completed. Bile from the liver (stored in the gall bladder) EMULSIFIES fats - breaks large fat droplets into tiny ones - and makes the medium alkaline. Pancreatic juice contains amylase (carbohydrates), trypsin (proteins) and lipase (fats). Intestinal juice completes the breakdown: carbohydrates -> glucose; proteins -> amino acids; fats -> fatty acids + glycerol.
 4. ABSORPTION: the digested food is absorbed into the blood through finger-like projections called VILLI that line the small intestine and greatly increase its surface area.
 5. ASSIMILATION: the absorbed nutrients are used by the body's cells for energy, growth and repair.
 6. EGESTION: undigested food passes into the large intestine, where water is absorbed, and the remaining waste (faeces) is removed through the anus.
ENZYMES are biological catalysts that speed up digestion; each acts on a specific type of food (amylase on starch, pepsin/trypsin on proteins, lipase on fats).

22.2 RESPIRATION

Respiration is the process by which food (mainly glucose) is broken down inside cells to RELEASE ENERGY. This energy is stored in molecules of ATP (adenosine triphosphate), the energy currency of the cell. Respiration is of two types depending on whether oxygen is used.
AEROBIC RESPIRATION uses oxygen and completely breaks glucose down to carbon dioxide and water, releasing a large amount of energy:

   C6H12O6 + 6O2 --> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP)

ANAEROBIC RESPIRATION takes place without oxygen and releases much less energy. In yeast, glucose is converted to ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide (this is FERMENTATION):

   C6H12O6 --> 2 C2H5OH + 2CO2 + energy

In our muscle cells during heavy exercise (when oxygen runs short), glucose is converted to LACTIC ACID:

   C6H12O6 --> 2 lactic acid + energy

The build-up of lactic acid causes muscle cramps.
GLYCOLYSIS: the first step common to both types is glycolysis, in which one glucose molecule (6 carbons) is split in the cytoplasm into two molecules of pyruvate (3 carbons each), releasing a little energy. In aerobic respiration pyruvate then enters the MITOCHONDRIA (the 'powerhouse of the cell') and is fully oxidised; in anaerobic respiration pyruvate is converted to ethanol or lactic acid.
BREATHING vs RESPIRATION: breathing (also called ventilation) is only the physical taking-in of air (inhalation) and giving-out of air (exhalation). Respiration is the chemical release of energy from food inside the cells. Breathing supplies the oxygen that cellular respiration needs.
HUMAN RESPIRATORY SYSTEM: air enters through the NOSTRILS -> nasal cavity (where it is filtered, warmed and moistened) -> pharynx -> LARYNX (voice box) -> TRACHEA (windpipe) -> two BRONCHI -> bronchioles -> tiny air sacs called ALVEOLI in the LUNGS. The DIAPHRAGM (a sheet of muscle below the lungs) and the rib muscles change the chest volume to draw air in and push it out.
EXCHANGE OF GASES: the alveoli are thin-walled and surrounded by blood capillaries. Oxygen from inhaled air diffuses into the blood (where it binds to haemoglobin in red blood cells), and carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli to be breathed out. The huge number of alveoli gives a very large surface area for this exchange.

22.3 TRANSPORTATION

Transportation carries materials around the body of a multicellular organism.
TRANSPORTATION IN PLANTS: plants have two conducting (vascular) tissues.
 - XYLEM carries WATER and dissolved minerals UPWARD from the roots to the leaves. The main force is the TRANSPIRATION PULL: water evaporates from the leaf surface (transpiration) through the stomata, creating a suction that pulls a continuous column of water up the xylem.
 - PHLOEM carries FOOD (sugars made in the leaves) to all other parts of the plant - this is called TRANSLOCATION. Unlike xylem flow, translocation can move in different directions and requires energy.
TRANSPORTATION IN HUMANS: humans have a CIRCULATORY SYSTEM made of blood, blood vessels and the heart.
BLOOD is a fluid connective tissue. Its components are: (1) PLASMA - the pale-yellow liquid (about 55%) that carries dissolved food, wastes, hormones and gases; (2) RED BLOOD CELLS (RBCs / erythrocytes) - contain HAEMOGLOBIN and carry oxygen; (3) WHITE BLOOD CELLS (WBCs / leucocytes) - fight infection and provide immunity; (4) PLATELETS (thrombocytes) - help in clotting of blood at a wound.
BLOOD VESSELS are of three kinds: ARTERIES carry blood AWAY from the heart (usually oxygenated, under high pressure, with thick elastic walls and no valves); VEINS carry blood TOWARD the heart (usually deoxygenated, under low pressure, with thinner walls and valves to prevent back-flow); CAPILLARIES are extremely thin one-cell-thick vessels where the actual exchange of materials with the tissues takes place.
THE HUMAN HEART is a muscular pump with FOUR CHAMBERS: two upper ATRIA (right and left) and two lower VENTRICLES (right and left). The right side handles deoxygenated blood; the left side handles oxygenated blood. Valves between the chambers (and at the vessel openings) prevent back-flow.
DOUBLE CIRCULATION: in humans, blood passes through the heart TWICE in one complete round. (1) PULMONARY circulation: the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the LUNGS, where it picks up oxygen and returns to the left atrium. (2) SYSTEMIC circulation: the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the whole BODY, and the deoxygenated blood returns to the right atrium. Because oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept completely separate, double circulation is very efficient and supports the high energy needs of warm-blooded animals.
LYMPH is a colourless fluid that leaks out of the blood capillaries into the tissues. It carries digested fats and drains excess fluid back into the blood. It is part of the body's immune defence.

22.4 EXCRETION

Excretion is the removal of harmful metabolic wastes, especially nitrogenous wastes such as urea, from the body.
EXCRETION IN PLANTS: plants do not have a special excretory system. They get rid of wastes in several ways - oxygen and carbon dioxide diffuse out through stomata; excess water is lost by transpiration; some wastes are stored in leaves, bark or old xylem and are shed when leaves or bark fall; resins and gums are stored in old tissues.
EXCRETION IN HUMANS: the main excretory organs are the two KIDNEYS, along with the ureters, urinary bladder and urethra (together the excretory or urinary system). The kidneys filter the blood and remove urea, excess water and salts as URINE.
THE NEPHRON is the structural and functional unit of the kidney; each kidney has about a million nephrons. A nephron has a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule enclosing a knot of capillaries called the GLOMERULUS, followed by a long coiled tubule.
URINE FORMATION takes place in three steps: (1) FILTRATION - blood is filtered under pressure at the glomerulus, and water, glucose, salts and urea pass into the Bowman's capsule as filtrate; (2) REABSORPTION - as the filtrate flows through the tubule, useful substances (most water, all glucose and useful salts) are reabsorbed back into the blood; (3) what remains - mainly urea, excess salts and water - becomes URINE, which passes down the ureters to the urinary bladder and is removed through the urethra.
DIALYSIS: when the kidneys fail, wastes build up in the blood. An artificial kidney machine carries out DIALYSIS - the patient's blood is passed through tubes made of a selectively permeable membrane surrounded by a dialysing fluid; wastes such as urea diffuse out of the blood into the fluid, and the cleaned blood is returned to the body.

SUMMARY

- Life processes are the basic functions (nutrition, respiration, transportation, excretion) that keep organisms alive.
- Autotrophs make food by photosynthesis (6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2, using sunlight and chlorophyll); heterotrophs are holozoic, saprophytic or parasitic.
- In humans, food is digested along the alimentary canal with the help of enzymes and glands, then absorbed by villi, assimilated, and the waste egested.
- Respiration releases energy from glucose; it is aerobic (with oxygen, more energy) or anaerobic (without oxygen, less energy, giving alcohol in yeast or lactic acid in muscle). Breathing is only the exchange of air; respiration is the cellular release of energy.
- In plants, xylem carries water up by transpiration pull and phloem translocates food. In humans, blood (plasma, RBC, WBC, platelets) flows through arteries, veins and capillaries pumped by a four-chambered heart in a double circulation.
- Excretion removes nitrogenous wastes; in humans the kidney's nephrons form urine by filtration and reabsorption, and dialysis substitutes for failed kidneys.

topics.name: Autotrophic Nutrition and Photosynthesis
topics.description: Autotrophic nutrition; photosynthesis - raw materials, site (chloroplast), the equation 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2, light and dark reactions, and the factors that affect the rate.

topics.name: Heterotrophic Nutrition and Human Digestion
topics.description: Holozoic, saprophytic and parasitic nutrition; the human alimentary canal and digestive glands; digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats by enzymes; absorption by villi, assimilation and egestion.

topics.name: Respiration in Organisms
topics.description: Aerobic vs anaerobic respiration with equations; glycolysis; the difference between breathing and respiration; the human respiratory system and exchange of gases in the alveoli.

topics.name: Transportation in Plants
topics.description: Conduction in plants: xylem carries water and minerals upward by transpiration pull; phloem translocates food made in the leaves to the rest of the plant.

topics.name: Transportation in Humans (Blood and Heart)
topics.description: Blood and its components (plasma, RBC, WBC, platelets); arteries, veins and capillaries; the four-chambered human heart; double circulation; and lymph.

topics.name: Excretion
topics.description: Removal of nitrogenous wastes: excretion in plants; the human excretory system, the nephron, the three steps of urine formation, and dialysis for kidney failure.

learning_outcomes.description: Describe autotrophic nutrition and explain photosynthesis - its raw materials, site, equation, light and dark reactions and the factors affecting its rate.
Distinguish holozoic, saprophytic and parasitic nutrition and trace the digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion of food in the human digestive system.
Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration with their equations and distinguish breathing from cellular respiration, outlining the role of glycolysis.
Describe the human respiratory system and explain the exchange of gases in the alveoli.
Explain transport in plants - the upward movement of water and minerals in xylem by transpiration pull and the translocation of food in phloem.
Describe blood and its components, the types of blood vessels, the structure of the human heart, and explain double circulation.
Explain excretion in plants and in humans, including the structure of the nephron and the steps of urine formation.
Explain the three steps of urine formation in the nephron (filtration, reabsorption, urine) and the principle of dialysis.

chapter_summary.title: Life Processes - 1: Nutrition, Transportation, Respiration and Excretion - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) summary for Lesson 22 covers four life processes: how organisms obtain food (nutrition and digestion), release energy from it (respiration), move materials around the body (transportation in plants and humans), and remove wastes (excretion).

details: Human digestion: alimentary canal + glands + enzymes

branches.label: Respiration
details: Aerobic: glucose + O2 -> CO2 + water + energy
Breathing vs respiration; alveoli exchange gases

branches.label: Transport in plants
details: Xylem: water and minerals up by transpiration pull

sections.heading: Nutrition: autotrophic and photosynthesis
bullets: Nutrition is taking in and using food. Autotrophs (green plants) make their own food; heterotrophs depend on others.
Photosynthesis: 6CO2 + 6H2O --(sunlight, chlorophyll)--> C6H12O6 + 6O2. Raw materials are CO2 (via stomata), water (from roots), sunlight and chlorophyll.
It occurs in chloroplasts and has a light reaction (splits water, releases oxygen) and a dark reaction (builds glucose from CO2).
Rate of photosynthesis is affected by light intensity, CO2 concentration, temperature and water.

sections.heading: Heterotrophic nutrition and human digestion
bullets: Heterotrophic nutrition is holozoic (taking in and digesting food, as in humans and Amoeba), saprophytic (on dead matter, as in fungi) or parasitic (on a living host, as in tapeworm).
The human alimentary canal runs mouth -> oesophagus -> stomach -> small intestine -> large intestine -> anus, with salivary glands, liver and pancreas as helpers.
Enzymes digest food: amylase on starch, pepsin and trypsin on proteins, lipase on fats; bile emulsifies fats.
Digested food is absorbed by villi in the small intestine, assimilated by cells, and undigested matter is egested.

sections.heading: Respiration
bullets: Respiration releases energy (ATP) from glucose. Aerobic respiration uses oxygen: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy.
Anaerobic respiration needs no oxygen and gives less energy - ethanol + CO2 in yeast, lactic acid in muscle (causing cramps).
Glycolysis splits glucose into pyruvate in the cytoplasm; aerobic respiration then completes in the mitochondria.
Breathing is the physical exchange of air; respiration is the chemical release of energy in cells. Air travels nostrils -> trachea -> bronchi -> alveoli, where gases are exchanged.

sections.heading: Transportation in plants and humans
bullets: In plants, xylem carries water and minerals upward by transpiration pull; phloem translocates food made in the leaves.
Human blood has plasma, red blood cells (carry oxygen via haemoglobin), white blood cells (immunity) and platelets (clotting).
Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins carry it back (with valves); capillaries are where exchange occurs.
The four-chambered heart drives double circulation: pulmonary (heart-lungs-heart) and systemic (heart-body-heart), keeping oxygenated and deoxygenated blood separate.

sections.heading: Excretion
bullets: Excretion removes nitrogenous wastes such as urea. Plants lose wastes through stomata, transpiration and by shedding leaves and bark.
In humans the kidneys filter the blood; the nephron is the functional unit, with a glomerulus in a Bowman's capsule and a long tubule.
Urine forms by filtration at the glomerulus, reabsorption of useful substances in the tubule, leaving urea, salts and water as urine.
When kidneys fail, dialysis uses an artificial kidney machine to remove wastes from the blood across a selectively permeable membrane.

key_takeaways: Life processes - nutrition, respiration, transportation and excretion - are the basic functions that keep all organisms alive.
Autotrophs photosynthesise (6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2 using sunlight and chlorophyll); heterotrophs are holozoic, saprophytic or parasitic.
In humans, enzymes and glands digest food along the alimentary canal; villi absorb it, cells assimilate it, and waste is egested.
Aerobic respiration (with oxygen) releases more energy than anaerobic respiration; breathing only exchanges air while respiration releases energy in cells.
Plants use xylem (water, by transpiration pull) and phloem (food); humans use blood, vessels and a four-chambered heart with double circulation.
The kidney's nephrons form urine by filtration and reabsorption; dialysis replaces failed kidney function.

glossary.definition: A basic function (nutrition, respiration, transportation, excretion, etc.) carried out by living organisms to stay alive.
The process by which green plants make glucose from CO2 and water using sunlight and chlorophyll: 6CO2 + 6H2O -> C6H12O6 + 6O2.
The green pigment in chloroplasts that traps sunlight for photosynthesis.
An organism, such as a green plant, that makes its own food from simple inorganic substances.
An organism that cannot make its own food and depends, directly or indirectly, on autotrophs.
A biological catalyst that speeds up a chemical reaction such as digestion; each enzyme acts on a specific substance.
Tiny finger-like projections lining the small intestine that increase surface area for the absorption of digested food.
Breakdown of glucose using oxygen to give CO2, water and a large amount of energy.
Breakdown of glucose without oxygen, giving less energy plus ethanol (in yeast) or lactic acid (in muscle).
The suction created by evaporation of water from leaves that pulls water up the xylem from the roots.
The plant tissue that transports (translocates) food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.
Circulation in which blood passes through the heart twice per cycle - pulmonary (heart-lungs) and systemic (heart-body).
The red pigment in red blood cells that binds and carries oxygen around the body.
The structural and functional unit of the kidney, where blood is filtered and urine is formed.
Use of an artificial kidney machine to remove wastes from the blood when the kidneys fail.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Life Processes - 1 (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) worksheet for Lesson 22. Attempt all questions. Write balanced word equations where asked and draw labelled diagrams where helpful.

questions.question: Write the balanced equation for photosynthesis and name the raw materials and the site where it occurs.
questions.answer:
Equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O --(sunlight, chlorophyll)--> C6H12O6 + 6O2.
Raw materials: carbon dioxide (from the air through stomata), water (absorbed by the roots) and sunlight (energy), with chlorophyll trapping the light.
Site: the chloroplasts of the green cells of the leaf.
questions.explanation: Recall equation, raw materials and site.

questions.question: Differentiate between the light reaction and the dark reaction of photosynthesis.
questions.answer:
Light reaction (light-dependent): occurs in the presence of light; chlorophyll absorbs sunlight; water is split (photolysis) releasing oxygen; energy is trapped in energy-rich molecules.
Dark reaction (light-independent): does not directly need light; the trapped energy is used to combine CO2 with hydrogen to form glucose.

questions.question: Distinguish between holozoic, saprophytic and parasitic nutrition with one example each.
questions.answer:
Holozoic: taking in solid/liquid food and digesting it inside the body - e.g. humans, Amoeba.
Saprophytic: feeding on dead and decaying matter by secreting enzymes onto it and absorbing the products - e.g. fungi (mushroom).
Parasitic: living on or in a host and taking food from it, harming it - e.g. tapeworm, Cuscuta.

questions.question: Trace the path of food through the human alimentary canal and state where carbohydrates, proteins and fats are digested and by which enzymes.
questions.answer:
Path: mouth -> oesophagus -> stomach -> small intestine -> large intestine -> rectum -> anus.
Carbohydrates: starch digestion begins in the mouth (salivary amylase) and is completed in the small intestine (pancreatic and intestinal amylase) to glucose.
Proteins: digestion begins in the stomach (pepsin in acidic medium) and is completed in the small intestine (trypsin) to amino acids.
Fats: bile from the liver emulsifies fats in the small intestine; lipase (from the pancreas and intestine) breaks them into fatty acids and glycerol.
Digested food is absorbed by villi, assimilated by cells, and the undigested waste is egested through the anus.
questions.explanation: Path plus site and enzyme for each food type.

questions.question: Write the equations for aerobic respiration and for anaerobic respiration in muscle and in yeast.
questions.answer:
Aerobic: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy (ATP).
Anaerobic in muscle: C6H12O6 -> 2 lactic acid + energy.
Anaerobic in yeast: C6H12O6 -> 2 C2H5OH + 2CO2 + energy.

questions.question: Distinguish between breathing and respiration.
questions.answer: Breathing (ventilation) is the physical process of taking air into the lungs (inhalation) and giving it out (exhalation); no energy is released. Respiration is the chemical process in which glucose is broken down inside cells to release energy (ATP). Breathing supplies the oxygen that respiration uses.

questions.question: Explain how water rises from the roots to the leaves of a tall tree.
questions.answer: Water rises mainly by TRANSPIRATION PULL. Water evaporates from the leaf surface through the stomata (transpiration). This creates a suction (negative pressure) in the leaf that pulls up a continuous, unbroken column of water through the XYLEM from the roots, helped by the cohesion of water molecules. Root pressure contributes a little, especially at night.

questions.question: Describe the structure of the human heart and explain double circulation.
questions.answer:
The human heart is a muscular pump with four chambers: two upper atria (right and left) and two lower ventricles (right and left). The right side carries deoxygenated blood and the left side carries oxygenated blood; valves prevent back-flow.
Double circulation: blood passes through the heart twice per cycle. (1) Pulmonary circulation - the right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs, where it is oxygenated, and it returns to the left atrium. (2) Systemic circulation - the left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body, and deoxygenated blood returns to the right atrium. Keeping the two streams separate makes circulation efficient and supports a high energy requirement.
questions.explanation: Four chambers + pulmonary and systemic loops.

questions.question: Name the components of blood and state one function of each.
questions.answer:
Plasma: liquid part that carries dissolved food, wastes, hormones and gases.
Red blood cells (RBCs): carry oxygen using haemoglobin.
White blood cells (WBCs): fight infection and provide immunity.
Platelets: help blood to clot at a wound.

questions.question: Describe the structure of a nephron and explain the three steps of urine formation. What is dialysis?
questions.answer:
A nephron is the functional unit of the kidney. It has a cup-shaped Bowman's capsule enclosing a knot of capillaries (the glomerulus) followed by a long coiled tubule.
Urine formation: (1) Filtration - blood is filtered under pressure at the glomerulus; water, glucose, salts and urea pass into the Bowman's capsule. (2) Reabsorption - as the filtrate flows along the tubule, useful substances (most water, all glucose, useful salts) are reabsorbed into the blood. (3) The remaining urea, excess salts and water form urine, which passes via the ureter to the bladder and out through the urethra.
Dialysis: when the kidneys fail, an artificial kidney machine passes the patient's blood across a selectively permeable membrane bathed in dialysing fluid; wastes such as urea diffuse out, and the cleaned blood is returned.

Deoxygenated blood from the body is pumped to the lungs by the
questions.explanation: Pulmonary circulation starts at the right ventricle.

questions.question: Oxygenated blood is pumped to the whole body by the
questions.explanation: Systemic circulation starts at the left ventricle.

questions.question: The colourless fluid that drains from tissues and aids immunity is
questions.explanation: Lymph carries fats and excess fluid.

questions.question: The main excretory organs in humans are the
questions.explanation: Kidneys filter blood and form urine.

questions.question: Which nitrogenous waste is removed in human urine?
questions.explanation: Urea is the main nitrogenous waste.

questions.question: Plants get rid of gaseous wastes mainly through the
The functional unit of the kidney is the

Cleaning the blood by an artificial kidney machine is called
Glucose is normally absent from urine because it is

questions.question: Oxygen is a raw material for photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Oxygen is a product, not a raw material; CO2 and water are the raw materials.

questions.question: Chlorophyll traps light energy for photosynthesis.
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll is the green pigment that absorbs sunlight.

questions.question: Bile contains digestive enzymes that break down fats.
questions.explanation: Bile contains no enzymes; it only emulsifies fats. Lipase digests them.

questions.question: Digestion of starch begins in the mouth.
Breathing and respiration are the same process.
questions.explanation: Breathing is the exchange of air; respiration releases energy in cells.

questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration releases far more energy.

questions.explanation: Xylem carries water up; phloem carries food.

questions.explanation: Arteries carry blood away from the heart.

questions.explanation: The four-chambered heart keeps the two streams apart.

questions.question: The nephron is the functional unit of the kidney.

questions.question: The balanced equation of photosynthesis is 6CO2 + 6H2O -> ____ + 6O2.
Photosynthesis occurs in the cell organelle called the ____.
The splitting of water in the light reaction is called ____.
The enzyme in saliva that digests starch is ____.
Fats are emulsified in the small intestine by ____.
questions.explanation: Bile from the liver emulsifies fats.

questions.question: Digested food is absorbed through the ____ of the small intestine.
The energy released in respiration is stored in molecules of ____.
Anaerobic respiration in muscle produces ____ acid.
Gas exchange in the lungs takes place in the ____.
Water rises up the xylem mainly because of the ____ pull.
The transport of food through phloem is called ____.
The red pigment in red blood cells is ____.
The human heart has ____ chambers.
The main nitrogenous waste removed in human urine is ____.
questions.explanation: Urea is the chief nitrogenous waste.

questions.question: The first step of urine formation, in which blood is filtered at the glomerulus, is called ____.
Define photosynthesis and write its overall equation.
questions.answer: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants make glucose from carbon dioxide and water using light energy trapped by chlorophyll. Equation: 6CO2 + 6H2O --(sunlight, chlorophyll)--> C6H12O6 + 6O2.

questions.question: Name the raw materials required for photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Carbon dioxide (from the air through stomata), water (absorbed by the roots), sunlight (the energy source) and chlorophyll (the green pigment that traps light).

questions.question: Explain the role of the light reaction and the dark reaction in photosynthesis.
questions.answer: In the light reaction (light-dependent), chlorophyll absorbs sunlight; the energy splits water (photolysis), releasing oxygen and trapping energy in energy-rich molecules. In the dark reaction (light-independent), this trapped energy is used to combine carbon dioxide with hydrogen to build glucose. The dark reaction does not directly require light.

questions.question: List the factors that affect the rate of photosynthesis.
questions.answer: Light intensity, concentration of carbon dioxide, temperature and availability of water. Within limits, increasing each of the first three increases the rate of photosynthesis.

questions.question: Distinguish between autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition with examples.
questions.answer: Autotrophic nutrition: the organism makes its own food from simple inorganic substances using light (e.g. green plants). Heterotrophic nutrition: the organism cannot make its own food and depends on others (e.g. animals, fungi). Autotrophs are producers; heterotrophs are consumers or decomposers.

questions.question: Name the three types of heterotrophic nutrition with one example each.
questions.answer: Holozoic (humans, Amoeba), saprophytic (fungi such as mushrooms), and parasitic (tapeworm, Cuscuta).

questions.question: Describe the role of the stomach in digestion.
questions.answer: In the stomach, gastric glands secrete gastric juice containing hydrochloric acid, the enzyme pepsin and mucus. HCl provides an acidic medium and kills germs; pepsin begins the digestion of proteins; mucus protects the stomach lining. Churning movements mix the food thoroughly with the juice.

questions.question: What is the role of bile in digestion? Where is it made?
questions.answer: Bile is made in the liver and stored in the gall bladder. It contains no enzymes but EMULSIFIES fats - breaking large fat droplets into tiny ones so enzymes can act on them - and makes the medium alkaline in the small intestine.

questions.question: State the final digestion products of carbohydrates, proteins and fats, and where absorption occurs.
questions.answer: Carbohydrates -> glucose; proteins -> amino acids; fats -> fatty acids and glycerol. Absorption of these products takes place in the small intestine through the finger-like villi, which provide a large surface area.

questions.question: Differentiate between absorption and assimilation.
questions.answer: Absorption is the passage of digested food from the small intestine into the blood (through the villi). Assimilation is the use of the absorbed nutrients by the body's cells for energy, growth and repair.

questions.question: Name the parts of the human alimentary canal in order.
questions.answer: Mouth -> oesophagus (food pipe) -> stomach -> small intestine -> large intestine -> rectum -> anus.

questions.question: Define respiration and name its two types.
questions.answer: Respiration is the process by which food (mainly glucose) is broken down inside cells to release energy (stored as ATP). Its two types are aerobic respiration (with oxygen) and anaerobic respiration (without oxygen).

questions.question: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration.
questions.answer: Aerobic respiration uses oxygen, fully breaks glucose into CO2 and water, and releases a large amount of energy: C6H12O6 + 6O2 -> 6CO2 + 6H2O + energy. Anaerobic respiration occurs without oxygen, only partly breaks glucose, and releases little energy - giving ethanol and CO2 in yeast, or lactic acid in muscle.

questions.question: What is glycolysis and where does it occur?
questions.answer: Glycolysis is the first step of respiration in which one glucose molecule (6 carbons) is split in the CYTOPLASM into two molecules of pyruvate (3 carbons each), releasing a small amount of energy. It is common to both aerobic and anaerobic respiration.

questions.question: Why do muscles ache after vigorous exercise?
questions.answer: During vigorous exercise the muscles do not get enough oxygen, so they respire anaerobically and produce LACTIC ACID. The build-up of lactic acid in the muscles causes cramps and aching.

questions.question: Give two differences between breathing and respiration.
questions.answer: (1) Breathing is a physical process (taking in and giving out air); respiration is a chemical process (breakdown of glucose to release energy). (2) Breathing occurs in the lungs/respiratory organs; respiration occurs inside the cells. Breathing supplies the oxygen used in respiration.

questions.question: Trace the path of air from the nostrils to the lungs.
questions.answer: Nostrils -> nasal cavity -> pharynx -> larynx -> trachea (windpipe) -> two bronchi -> bronchioles -> alveoli in the lungs.

questions.question: Explain how the exchange of gases takes place in the alveoli.
questions.answer: The alveoli are thin-walled air sacs surrounded by blood capillaries. Oxygen from the inhaled air diffuses across the thin wall into the blood, where it binds to haemoglobin in the red blood cells. At the same time, carbon dioxide diffuses from the blood into the alveoli and is breathed out. The large number of alveoli provides a very large surface area for rapid diffusion.

questions.question: Name the structure that carries oxygen in blood and state the gas it carries away from tissues.
questions.answer: Oxygen is carried by HAEMOGLOBIN in the red blood cells. The waste gas carried away from the tissues is carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Name the two conducting tissues in plants and state what each transports.
questions.answer: Xylem - transports water and dissolved minerals upward from roots to leaves. Phloem - transports (translocates) food made in the leaves to other parts of the plant.

questions.question: Explain the transpiration pull and how it moves water up a tall plant.
questions.answer: Water evaporates from the leaf surface through the stomata (transpiration). This loss creates a suction or negative pressure in the leaf cells, which pulls up a continuous, unbroken column of water through the xylem from the roots. The cohesion (sticking together) of water molecules keeps the column intact. This force is strong enough to raise water in even very tall trees.

questions.question: How does transport in phloem differ from transport in xylem?
questions.answer: Xylem carries water and minerals only upward, using the passive transpiration pull. Phloem carries food (sugars) and can move it in different directions (up or down to wherever it is needed), and this translocation requires energy.

questions.question: Name the four components of blood.
questions.answer: Plasma (liquid part), red blood cells (RBCs), white blood cells (WBCs) and platelets.

questions.question: State three differences between arteries and veins.
questions.answer: (1) Arteries carry blood AWAY from the heart; veins carry it TOWARD the heart. (2) Arteries usually carry oxygenated blood (except the pulmonary artery); veins usually carry deoxygenated blood (except the pulmonary vein). (3) Arteries have thick elastic walls and no valves and carry blood at high pressure; veins have thinner walls, valves to prevent back-flow, and carry blood at low pressure.

questions.question: What is double circulation? Why is it advantageous?
questions.answer: Double circulation means that blood passes through the heart twice in one complete cycle: pulmonary circulation (right ventricle -> lungs -> left atrium) and systemic circulation (left ventricle -> body -> right atrium). It is advantageous because oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept completely separate, making oxygen delivery efficient. This supports the high energy needs of warm-blooded animals.

questions.question: What is lymph and what are its functions?
questions.answer: Lymph is a colourless fluid that leaks from the blood capillaries into the tissue spaces. It carries digested fats, drains excess fluid back into the blood, and forms part of the body's immune defence.

questions.question: How do plants get rid of their wastes?
questions.answer: Plants have no special excretory system. Gaseous wastes (oxygen and carbon dioxide) diffuse out through stomata; excess water is lost by transpiration; some wastes are stored in leaves, bark and old xylem and are removed when these parts are shed; resins and gums are stored in old tissues.

questions.question: Name the organs of the human excretory (urinary) system.
questions.answer: Two kidneys, two ureters, the urinary bladder and the urethra.

questions.question: Describe the three steps of urine formation in the nephron.
questions.answer: (1) Filtration - blood is filtered under pressure at the glomerulus, and water, glucose, salts and urea pass into the Bowman's capsule. (2) Reabsorption - as the filtrate flows through the tubule, useful substances (most water, all glucose and useful salts) are reabsorbed into the blood. (3) The remaining urea, excess salts and water form urine, which passes to the bladder and is removed through the urethra.

questions.question: What is dialysis and when is it needed?
questions.answer: Dialysis is the cleaning of the blood by an artificial kidney machine when a person's kidneys fail. The blood is passed through tubes of a selectively permeable membrane surrounded by dialysing fluid; wastes such as urea diffuse out of the blood into the fluid, and the cleaned blood is returned to the body.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A green plant is kept in bright sunlight. Bubbles of gas are seen rising from a water plant placed in a beaker. The leaf cells contain a green pigment that traps sunlight.

(i) Name the process taking place.
(ii) Name the gas in the bubbles.
(iii) Write the balanced equation for the process.
(iv) Name the green pigment and where it is located.
questions.answer:
(i) Photosynthesis.
(ii) Oxygen.
(iii) 6CO2 + 6H2O --(sunlight, chlorophyll)--> C6H12O6 + 6O2.
(iv) The green pigment is chlorophyll, located in the chloroplasts of the leaf cells.
questions.explanation: Apply the photosynthesis concept to an experiment.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

After a meal of bread, dal and butter, the food passes along the alimentary canal. Different enzymes act at different places.

(i) Which enzyme starts the digestion of the starch in the bread, and where?
(ii) Where does the digestion of the protein in the dal begin?
(iii) Which secretion emulsifies the butter (fat)?
(iv) Where is the digested food absorbed?
questions.answer:
(i) Salivary amylase, in the mouth.
(ii) In the stomach, by pepsin in an acidic medium.
(iii) Bile (from the liver) emulsifies the fat in the small intestine.
(iv) In the small intestine, through the villi.
questions.explanation: Apply digestion sites and enzymes to a real meal.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A sprinter runs a 100 m race at full speed. Soon her leg muscles begin to ache. A jar of fruit juice left with yeast turns fizzy and smells of alcohol.

(i) What type of respiration occurs in the sprinter's muscles?
(ii) Which substance causes the ache?
(iii) What does the yeast produce?
(iv) Which type of respiration releases more energy, and why?
questions.answer:
(i) Anaerobic respiration (because oxygen is in short supply during fast running).
(ii) Lactic acid, which builds up in the muscles.
(iii) Yeast produces ethanol (alcohol) and carbon dioxide (fermentation) - hence the fizz and smell.
(iv) Aerobic respiration releases more energy, because glucose is completely broken down to CO2 and water; anaerobic respiration only partly breaks it down.
questions.explanation: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration in context.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

When we breathe in, air travels through a series of tubes to reach tiny sacs in the lungs where gases are exchanged with the blood.

(i) Name, in order, the tubes air passes through from the windpipe to the air sacs.
(ii) Name the air sacs.
(iii) Which gas passes from the air sacs into the blood, and which passes the other way?
(iv) Why are the air sacs so numerous and thin-walled?
questions.answer:
(i) Trachea (windpipe) -> two bronchi -> bronchioles -> alveoli.
(ii) The air sacs are the alveoli.
(iii) Oxygen passes from the alveoli into the blood; carbon dioxide passes from the blood into the alveoli.
(iv) Being numerous and thin-walled gives a very large surface area and a short diffusion distance, so gases are exchanged rapidly and efficiently.
questions.explanation: Apply the respiratory pathway and gas exchange.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A tall tree carries water from its roots all the way up to its topmost leaves, and carries the sugar made in the leaves down to the roots.

(i) Which tissue carries water upward?
(ii) What is the main force responsible?
(iii) Which tissue carries the sugar, and what is this transport called?
(iv) Why can the sugar move in more than one direction?
questions.answer:
(i) Xylem carries water (and minerals) upward.
(ii) The transpiration pull - the suction created when water evaporates from the leaves.
(iii) Phloem carries the sugar; the transport is called translocation.
(iv) Translocation is an energy-requiring process and food is sent wherever it is needed (growing tips, roots, fruits), so phloem can move it in different directions.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The human heart is a four-chambered pump. Blood goes from the heart to the lungs and back, and from the heart to the body and back.

(i) Name the four chambers of the heart.
(ii) Which chamber pumps blood to the lungs?
(iii) Which chamber pumps blood to the rest of the body?
(iv) What name is given to this pattern of circulation, and why is it efficient?
questions.answer:
(i) Right atrium, right ventricle, left atrium, left ventricle.
(ii) The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation).
(iii) The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood to the whole body (systemic circulation).
(iv) It is called double circulation. It is efficient because oxygenated and deoxygenated blood are kept completely separate, so the body always receives fully oxygenated blood.
questions.explanation: Analyse the heart and double circulation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Blood is a fluid connective tissue with a liquid part and several kinds of cells. It flows through three kinds of vessels.

(i) Name the liquid part of blood.
(ii) Which cells carry oxygen, and using which pigment?
(iii) Which cells help fight disease, and which help clotting?
(iv) Name the three kinds of blood vessels.
questions.answer:
(i) Plasma.
(ii) Red blood cells (RBCs) carry oxygen using the pigment haemoglobin.
(iii) White blood cells (WBCs) fight disease; platelets help clotting.
(iv) Arteries, veins and capillaries.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Each kidney contains about a million tiny filtering units. Blood is filtered, useful substances are taken back, and the rest leaves as urine.

(i) Name the filtering unit of the kidney.
(ii) Name the knot of capillaries where blood is filtered.
(iii) During which step are glucose and most water returned to the blood?
(iv) Why is there normally no glucose in the urine of a healthy person?
questions.answer:
(i) The nephron.
(ii) The glomerulus (inside the Bowman's capsule).
(iii) During reabsorption, as the filtrate flows through the tubule.
(iv) Because all the glucose filtered at the glomerulus is completely reabsorbed back into the blood during reabsorption, so none is left in the urine.
questions.explanation: Apply nephron structure and urine formation.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A patient's kidneys have stopped working, so wastes build up in his blood. Doctors connect him to an artificial kidney machine.

(i) What is this treatment called?
(ii) What is the chief waste that must be removed?
(iii) Across what kind of membrane does the waste pass?
(iv) Why does the waste move from the blood into the dialysing fluid?
questions.answer:
(i) Dialysis.
(ii) Urea (the main nitrogenous waste).
(iii) A selectively (semi-) permeable membrane.
(iv) The blood has a high concentration of urea and the dialysing fluid has none, so urea diffuses down the concentration gradient from the blood into the fluid; the cleaned blood is then returned.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

Three organisms are observed: a mushroom growing on a rotting log, a tapeworm inside a person's intestine, and an Amoeba engulfing a food particle.

(i) Name the type of nutrition in the mushroom.
(ii) Name the type of nutrition in the tapeworm.
(iii) Name the type of nutrition in the Amoeba.
(iv) Which of these three is harmful to another living organism?
questions.answer:
(i) Saprophytic nutrition (it feeds on dead, decaying matter).
(ii) Parasitic nutrition (it lives inside a host and takes its food).
(iii) Holozoic nutrition (it takes in and digests solid food).
(iv) The tapeworm, because it harms its host (the parasite's host).
